items.title: Me and My Agents
items.content:
Programming note: I’ll be attending the TomorrowX Summit in Austin in November, followed by Fintech Nerdcon in San Diego. If you’re at either, please say hi. 
 In my former career as a research analyst, I would approach earnings season with a mix of trepidation and excitement. The period – which kicked off this week in the banks sector – meant early starts and late nights. Companies report as early as 6am and I would need to be on standby to read the release. With filings stretching to 75 pages, there was a lot to absorb. I would need to communicate my thoughts to an internal salesforce and to institutional clients, and then update my model, dial in to the earnings call, ask three questions, revise my model and publish a note – all against the backdrop of a cutthroat Wall Street environment where a dozen other analysts were doing the same thing. Sometimes we’d juggle several earnings releases on the same day, and unless it was Friday, it’d start all over again the next morning.
 As an investor, the experience was less intense, though the stakes were higher. My time on the sell-side taught me what to look for in a release, so by the time I started managing money, I could process earnings much faster. It proved useful. Although they make up just 1.6% of trading days, earnings release dates account for 15% of annual share-price variance. Earnings revisions remain a key driver of stock performance and the market doesn’t always get them right. On more than a few occasions, I was able to exploit the heightened liquidity around announcements to act on my analysis before the market opened or while earnings calls were underway.
 This week, the six largest US banks reported third-quarter earnings. Collectively, they poured over 250 pages of financial information into the market and hosted over eight hours of calls to explain it. JPMorgan alone furnished investors with 523 new data points.
 These days, I’m fortunate to have a team to help me distill it all. I’ve trained four AI agents to parse earnings materials, and this week they earned their keep.
 Allow me to introduce them:
 Ernie does the heavy lifting. I have a folder on my desktop for each of the banks I follow, containing historic earnings releases, investor presentations, call transcripts and the latest annual report. When a new release lands, Ernie studies the folder, builds a picture of what the market is expecting from analyst previews and tells me where the quarter confirms that view and where it departs. Once the call transcript is in, Ernie incorporates it, delivering a five-page report and a two-page brief in the time it takes me to brew an espresso.
 Thelma tracks the themes I’m monitoring, collating new evidence as it emerges. Agentic disruption , AI financing and private credit are three that we’ve discussed here the past few weeks; the impact of rising rates is back on the list, too. Thelma flags what management is saying about each of them and what the underlying numbers show.
 My Mike Mayo bot previews the question Mike Mayo is most likely to ask on the call. I’ve profiled Mike here before. Currently working as an analyst at Wells Fargo Securities, Mike has covered banks through more than 140 earnings seasons, and his unflinching questions invariably surface the most pressing issues of the day.
 Finally, my earnings modeller updates my model directly in Excel. We road-tested AI modelling back in February in Excel Forever – it’s improved a lot since then.
 My agents were more impressed with earnings than the market seemed to be. Guidance was broadly up, in particular on higher net interest income. Equities trading and banking fees were mostly strong enough to offset a weaker period for fixed income trading. Consumers continued to spend and credit held up.
 But that only scratches the surface. Ernie, Thelma and the team turned up things I couldn’t have got to as quickly. To find out what they showed me and, more generally, how I trained them to do it, read on. Paid subscribers can also email me for access to the instructions I wrote for them and the outputs they produced.

items.title: When Saturday Comes
items.content:
I’ve told you about the time I owned a pub , but have I told you about the time I owned a football club?
 It was 1996 and an opportunity arose to invest in Liverpool FC. At the time, the club was majority owned by the Moores family, heirs to the Littlewoods retail and football betting fortune. David Moores, the club’s chairman, owned 51%.
 But Moores didn’t control all the shares. Since the club’s founding in 1892, a small minority had circulated among fans and individual investors. For a hundred years those shares weren’t easily transferable. They passed from generation to generation. If they were traded at all, it was through private negotiation.
 Then, in 1991, a London-based broker launched a platform with a mandate to trade unquoted stocks over the counter under Stock Exchange rules. Liverpool FC and Athletic Grounds PLC became one of the platform’s highest profile markets. After leaving a buy order with my own broker, I was eventually matched with a seller. For a consideration of £1950 (plus commission of 2.2%) I became the proud owner of a single share in Liverpool Football Club.
 My timing was fortuitous. “Pre Euro 96, football was incredibly unfashionable,” recalled Moores later. After England hosted the European championship that summer, though, the country went football mad. Within a few months, the value of my share had doubled. I’d never made so much money, so quickly and having just bought my first home, with all the budgetary pressures that entails, I sold.

 The one that got away 
 It’s a trade I would live to regret. Not that I sold too cheap. The club was taken over eleven years later at a price of £5000 a share, so I caught the big move. Indeed, prior to the flurry of takeover interest in 2007, the shares consistently traded below my exit price. For over a decade, their valuation didn’t grow.
 My regret came from what I gave up. To squeeze out the minorities, the club’s buyers, Tom Hicks and George Gillett, had to offer an inducement. They offered individual shareholders priority ticket purchasing rights, guaranteeing them lifetime access to home cup matches and cup finals. With Liverpool appearing in nine cup finals in the past ten years alone, those priority rights became a valuable asset I lost exposure to. 1 
 Still, my fleeting ownership of a single share in Liverpool FC gave me an insight into football club valuations. When I sold, the club had an equity value of £125 million. Eleven years later, Moores sold to Hicks and Gillett for £174 million – or £219 million including the £45 million of debt they took on. In 2010, the club changed hands again when Red Sox owners Fenway Sports Group bought it at a valuation of £300 million. Over the next 16 years, Liverpool’s valuation climbed steadily under FSG’s ownership. Then, in August, they sold a 38% stake to a consortium, 1892 Holdings, at a valuation of about £5.5 billion ($7.3 billion). Not a match for my IRR, but as a multiple on invested capital, not a bad return.

 Along the way, rising valuations have transformed the market for football club ownership. Old-school club owners – the locally-based, locally wealthy supporters like David Moores – have long been priced out. “With the influx of more and more overseas superstars on superstar wages, I was aware the game was changing beyond all recognition and deeply worried, too, about my ability to continue underwriting the financial side,” Moores reflected . “The Abramovich era was upon us, and I knew that I could never compete.”
 At current valuations, though, even oligarchs can’t compete. In 2010, every member of the Forbes 400 was wealthy enough to have bought Liverpool Football Club for less than half their net worth. Today, despite the enormous increase in global wealth over the intervening period, just 88 of them could do the same. 2 
 Sovereign wealth goes some way to fill the gap, but greater regulatory scrutiny and ongoing controversy surrounding Abu Dhabi’s ownership of Manchester City make this less likely going forward. Instead, a new source of capital is emerging: institutional private equity. According to the International Centre for Sports Studies, a fifth of the 92 clubs competing across the Premier League, the EFL Championship, and EFL Leagues One and Two have private capital represented within their shareholding structures, up from 8% in 2010. Within the Premier League, the fraction is 40%.
 It’s an area private equity firms are increasingly targeting. Earlier this year, KKR acquired Arctos Partners to give it a foothold in sports. Apollo launched Apollo Sports Capital as a distinct business. Sixth Street, TPG and Avenue have all actively raised funds for sports investment over the course of the last year.
 Apollo’s Al Tylis reckons it’s a new asset class. He estimates that across leagues, venues, media, merchandise, fitness and live events, sports is a $2.5 trillion market. KKR more narrowly puts the addressable market at $650 billion, but agrees with Apollo that it’s undercapitalized. KKR estimates private capital penetration in sports at just 2%.
 In English football the trend is visible with Clearlake Capital taking full control of Chelsea last month (at a valuation of £5 billion, equivalent to $6.7 billion). As an investor in Manchester City, Silver Lake will be keeping a close eye on developments there.
 But is football really a viable asset class? David Moores said of his ownership of Liverpool, “If we’d have done it as an ‘investment’ we’d have come unstuck pretty quickly.” Has the market changed? To explore the economics of football and understand what private equity sees in it, read on.

items.title: The Art of Doing Financial Engineering
items.content:
Every boom is accompanied by a parallel boom in financial engineering and this one is no exception. The scale demands it. Estimates for AI infrastructure capex through 2030 range between $7.6 trillion and $8.0 trillion, and while bond markets are deep, they’re not that deep.
 Analysts at KKR estimate that traditional US public investment-grade investors should be able to provide $1.7 trillion of financing – but that leaves a gap of $6.3 trillion. They predict it will be filled by a mix of financing instruments: private investment-grade debt, asset-backed finance, infrastructure debt, structured solutions “and financing structures that may not even exist yet.”
 There’s nothing new in this. AI capex could reach 3.63% of GDP out to 2032, but history offers a close parallel. Between 1870 and 1890, as rail infrastructure was laid at a frantic pace, associated capital expenditure amounted to 2.24% of GDP.
 In his book, Railroaded , Richard White describes the scene:
 “Investors proceeded from government bonds to government secured railroad bonds, to convertible bonds, to mortgage bonds vouched for by the same people who sold the government bonds, to a whole array of financial instruments, and from there, potentially, into the drink… There were first mortgage bonds and second mortgage bonds; there were mortgages on the trunk line and mortgages on the branches. There were land grant bonds and income bonds. There were bonds on anything and everything that investors might accept as collateral. The bankers as well as the railroads they represented trumpeted the security of these investments, but they were in effect so many carnival barkers.” 
 Financial engineering is a difficult quantity to measure, but its ebbs and flows are worth watching as a signal of where we are in the cycle. Like other forms of engineering, it can be used for good or ill. It tends to flourish when conventional balance sheets can no longer keep pace with an investment boom, but the structures that keep the boom going can also obscure where its risks are accumulating.
 One way to study it is through the eyes of the financial engineers who practise it. Their role is to navigate the demands of companies, investors, regulators, auditors and credit rating agencies to devise structures that allocate cash flows and risk among the parties most willing and able to bear them.
 To see what they’re up to, let’s take a look at their work. This week in Net Interest , we go deep inside some of the structures dreamt up by financial engineers this year. We visit Louisiana, Texas and Ohio, all via Wall Street. To explore with me, read on…
 Case 1: Hyperion In December 2024, Meta broke ground on a new data center complex in Richland Parish, Louisiana. The 2,250-acre site was to be a cornerstone of Mark Zuckerberg’s push into artificial intelligence. It “will be able to scale up to 5GW over several years,” he posted .

 Not as big as Manhattan, but close 
 The only problem: a project of this size requires a lot of money.
 Meta put the initial cost of the project at $10 billion and started to bankroll it using its own funds, but the scale of the project threatened to overwhelm its balance sheet, so it looked for other solutions. Enter the financial engineers of Morgan Stanley.

items.title: Agents Revolt
items.content:
Mark Zuckerberg has tried to disrupt the financial sector before. In 2019, he unveiled plans for a new currency, Libra. “What we’re trying to do,” he explained , “[is] rethink what a modern infrastructure for the financial system would be if you started it today rather than fifty years ago on a lot of outdated systems.”
 The industry didn’t respond kindly, and he backed down.
 Today, he comes again. This month, his company Meta launched Muse – “a secure, private personal AI agent that proactively helps with people’s goals and suggests ideas.” We’ve discussed AI agents before – notably in last November’s Agentic Friday about their spread through online shopping channels – but Muse has loftier ambitions. “It can handle tasks, like sending an email or booking travel,” Meta says, “and it can take on big audacious goals.”
 Already, people seem to like it. The app ​recorded 2.8 million downloads within two weeks of its launch, propelling it to number one on both Apple’s US App Store and Google Play, a faster start than ChatGPT managed. “The Muse reception has honestly been beyond our biggest dreams,” posted its creator Alexandr Wang.

 Source: Citi Research, Sensor Tower 
 I haven’t tried it yet – Muse is currently only available in the US and Canada – but I have been trialling Instinct, a similar app launched by startup Spear Street Technology, whose valuation has increased fourfold in less than a month. Instinct sits inside WhatsApp, which it uses as its interface, while a virtual desktop behind the scenes navigates websites and accesses email and calendar on your behalf.
 Having signed up, the first thing I did was ask it to find me cheaper car insurance. I won’t go into the details, but I’ve struggled to obtain good value coverage since my car was stolen a couple of years ago. It didn’t help that I carelessly replaced it with a model even more vulnerable to theft. My premium was already high but at the last renewal it jumped 83%. Instinct analysed my current policy, approached carriers for alternative quotes and offered to automate a switch to a cheaper policy, all while I slept.
 It seems I am not alone. One driver posted that Muse saved him $3,500 a year on auto insurance by gathering quotes and processing a switch from Liberty Mutual to Progressive on his behalf. Aggregator portals could have done the job, but the friction of an AI assistant was lower and the new policy matched the terms of his old one.
 Angela Strange, a partner at venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, reckons this is a big deal: “This is what Insurance companies (and banks) should be TERRIFIED about… Inertia and information asymmetry will no longer be enough to keep customers.”
 Muse promises to take on big audacious goals. Could one of those be to neutralise the inertia on which much of the finance industry’s margin depends? To find out which firms are most exposed, and which stand to gain, read on.
